en: Theravāda Vinaya Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga Pācittiyakaṇḍa
The Garlic Chapter 2.
The Training Rule on Pubic Hair.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the group-of-six bhikkhunīs had hair removed from their private parts and were bathing naked together with courtesans at a single bathing place in the Aciravatī River.
The courtesans complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying:
“How can these bhikkhunīs have hair removed from their private parts? They are just like householders who indulge in sensual pleasures!”
The bhikkhunīs heard those courtesans complaining, criticizing, and grumbling.
Those bhikkhunīs who were few in desires... [they] complained, criticized, and grumbled:
"How can the bhikkhunīs of the group of six have body hair removed from the private parts?"... [etc.]
“Is it true, monks, that the group-of-six bhikkhunīs have hair removed from their private parts?
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them … [as before] …
“How indeed, monks, can the group-of-six bhikkhunīs have hair removed from the private parts?
This, monks, is neither for the inspiration of those without faith nor for the increase of the faithful...
And thus, monks, should the bhikkhunīs recite this training rule:”
“Whatever nun should have hair removed from the private parts, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
“Whatever nun” means whichever nun of such a kind... [and so forth].
"A bhikkhunī" ...
[as before] ... this is the kind of bhikkhunī intended in this context.
"The private parts" (sambādha) means:
"Both armpits" and "the urinary organ.
"Should have it removed" means:
if she has even a single hair removed, there is an offense of *pācittiya*.
If she causes even many hairs to be plucked out, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
There is no offense if it is due to a medical condition.
"In the case of one who is insane,
or in the case of one who is a first-offender.
The second training rule is concluded.
